title: Biology: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank
html:
Group A of the Biology paper is eleven marks — five from Botany, six from Zoology — and it is the only part of the paper where a candidate who has read the book carefully can score full marks in twelve minutes.

This chapter is the drill for it.

Every syllabus unit of Grade 11 Biology gets its own bank of multiple-choice questions, an answer key that gives a reason rather than a letter, and a table of the facts that objective questions keep coming back to.

How to use this bank

Do not read the questions. Answer them, on paper, covering the key. Retrieval is what builds memory; recognition feels like learning and is not. Mark the ones you got wrong, and come back to only those after three days, then after ten.

The reason line in the key matters more than the letter — if you cannot say why the other three options are wrong, you have not finished the question.

36. (c) — rRNA is transcribed and packed with protein in the nucleolus.

37. (a) — metacentric gives equal arms and a V shape at anaphase; telocentric has the centromere at the very end.

38. (b) — interphase is about 90–95 % of the cycle; it is growth, not rest.

39. (b) — S for synthesis; after S the DNA content has doubled but the chromosome number has not.

40. (c) — mitosis is equational: 2n stays 2n, so 24 chromosomes in each of the two daughter cells.

41. (b) — meiosis is reductional: 2n = 24 gives n = 12 in each of the four cells. Answering 24 here and 12 in question 40 is the single commonest cell-division error in the board exam.

42. (c) — pachytene, when the bivalent has four chromatids and recombination nodules appear.

43. (c) — the homologues begin to separate at diplotene and the crossover points show as X-shaped chiasmata.

44. (a) — homologous pairs separate in anaphase I, halving the number; meiosis II merely separates sister chromatids.

45. (c) — amitosis, seen in Amoeba, bacteria, and in the foetal membranes and diseased cells of higher organisms.

The distractor that catches everyone: 2n versus n

Questions 40 and 41 are the same cell dividing two different ways.

Fix the two sentences in your head and never compute them again: mitosis — one cell, two daughters, 2n each, chromosomes identical to the parent. meiosis — one cell, four daughters, n each, chromosomes recombined. The number is halved once, in anaphase I, and nowhere else.

Meiosis II does not halve anything; it separates sister chromatids exactly as mitosis does, which is why it is called the equational division.

Reading a cell-division question

Problem. A pollen mother cell of a plant contains 36 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will be present in (i) each pollen grain, (ii) each cell of the tapetum dividing mitotically, (iii) the endosperm?

Solution. The pollen mother cell is diploid, so 2n = 36 and n = 18.

(i) A pollen grain is formed by meiosis, so it is haploid: 18. (ii) The tapetum is ordinary somatic tissue dividing by mitosis, which keeps the number: 36.

(iii) The endosperm of an angiosperm is triploid (one male nucleus plus two polar nuclei), so it has 3n = 3 \times 18 = 54.

The whole question is answered by knowing which cells are the products of which division. Never multiply or divide by 2 without first naming the division.

Telling the four families apart in one line each
  • Brassicaceae — four petals in a cross, six stamens 4 long + 2 short (tetradynamous), fruit a siliqua. Brassica, Raphanus.
  • Fabaceae — butterfly corolla, stamens (9) + 1 (diadelphous), one carpel, fruit a pod, root nodules. Pisum, Cicer.
  • Solanaceae — everything in fives, ovary bicarpellary and oblique, fruit a berry or capsule. Solanum, Capsicum.
  • Liliaceae — everything in threes, sepals and petals alike (tepals), a monocot. Allium, Asparagus.

An energy-flow calculation the way the board asks it

Problem. In a grassland the producers fix 9600\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} of solar energy and use 6400\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1} of it in their own respiration. Find the net primary productivity, and the energy that reaches a snake feeding on frogs.

Solution. First the productivity:

\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = 9600 - 6400 = 3200\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}

Only the NPP is available to the next trophic level. Now apply the ten per cent law step by step, naming the level each time:

  • grasshopper (2nd level): 0.10 \times 3200 = 320\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}
  • frog (3rd level): 0.10 \times 320 = 32\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}
  • snake (4th level): 0.10 \times 32 = 3.2\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}

So the snake receives 3.2\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}. Notice that the answer is taken from NPP, not from GPP — starting from 9600 would give 9.6 and lose the mark.

Homologous or analogous — decide by origin, not by job

Ask one question only: do the two organs have the same basic plan and the same embryonic origin? If yes they are homologous, whatever they are used for (a whale's flipper and your arm).

If no they are analogous, however alike they look (a butterfly's wing and a bird's wing). Homology means divergence from a shared ancestor; analogy means convergence on a shared job.

Which host is the primary host?

The primary (definitive) host is the one in which the parasite reproduces sexually. For Plasmodium the sexual cycle is completed in the mosquito, so the mosquito is the primary host and the human is the secondary (intermediate) host — even though the human is the one who is ill.

Deciding by "which one matters more to us" is what makes this the single most-missed one-mark question in Zoology.

Eliminating three options before you choose one

Problem. The primary host of Plasmodium is(a) man(b) female Anopheles mosquito(c) female Culex mosquito(d) housefly. Answer it without recalling the definition.

Solution. Work by elimination, which is faster and safer than recall.

Step 1 — use the biology you are sure of. Malaria is spread by Anopheles, not Culex (which spreads filariasis) and not the housefly (which spreads typhoid and cholera mechanically). Options (c) and (d) go at once.

Two options remain and the question is already worth half a mark in expectation.

Step 2 — find the discriminating rule. The remaining pair, man and mosquito, differ only in which cycle happens where.

The rule is: the definitive host is where the sexual cycle occurs. Gametocytes are taken up by the mosquito, and fertilisation and zygote formation happen in its gut.

Step 3 — apply and check. Sexual cycle in the mosquito, therefore the mosquito is primary, therefore (b).

Check the leftover man harbours the asexual schizogony, so man is the secondary host — which is consistent, so the answer stands.

Notice that steps 1 and 3 used ordinary content knowledge and only step 2 used the definition.

In a bank of 300 questions you will not recall every definition; you will almost always recall enough to delete two options, and a one-in-two guess across eleven MCQs is worth about five and a half marks.

This chapter is the objective half of your Biology revision: close to three hundred one-mark questions arranged unit by unit against the CDC Grade 11 syllabus, each with an answer key that gives the reason rather than the letter.

  • Group A of the NEB Biology paper carries eleven marks, five from Botany and six from Zoology, and is the only part of the paper where a wrong answer costs you the whole mark with no part credit. It is also the part most reliably won by practice.
  • The marks follow the teaching hours. Floral Diversity (30 h) and Faunal Diversity (34 h) together account for half the syllabus, and the number of questions in sections 8.2 and 8.8 is in proportion.
  • Most one-mark questions are decided by a single discriminating fact: 2n versus n, prokaryote versus eukaryote, homologous versus analogous, primary versus secondary host, endemic versus exotic, vulnerable versus endangered. The distractors in this bank are built from those exact confusions on purpose.
  • Where the answer key says "this is the one everyone misses", stop and write the pair out in your own words. Those boxes mark the questions that separate an A from an A+.
  • Use the bank as retrieval practice, not as reading. Cover the key, answer a whole section in one sitting against the clock (about thirty seconds a question), then mark it and read the reasons only for the ones you got wrong. Revisit those after two days and again after a week.
  • A question in this book carries a year tag only where the paper it came from could be verified. Everything untagged is either an original question written to the CDC grid or a question from an undated official release.

  1. Describe the structure of Paramecium caudatum with a labelled diagram and explain the process and significance of conjugation. [8]

Answers to Group A

1. (b) — mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, which is the evidence for the endosymbiotic theory.

2. (b) — meiosis I is the reduction division, so each of the two cells already has n = 12; the halving happens in the first division, not the second. This is the classic trap.

3. (c) — Solanaceae; the obliquely placed bicarpellary ovary is unique to the family.

4. (b) — TMV is a single-stranded RNA virus, the first virus ever crystallised.

5. (b) — Lindeman's ten per cent law; the remaining ninety per cent is lost as heat and in respiration.

6. (b) — homologous organs, showing divergent evolution from a common ancestor.

7. (b) — Paramecium, with a vegetative macronucleus and a generative micronucleus.

8. (b) — segments 14, 15 and 16, the girdle that secretes the cocoon.

9. (b) — the single ventricle; the spiral valve of the conus arteriosus reduces but does not prevent the mixing.

10. (b) — blubber, which insulates and adds buoyancy.

11. (c) — Chitwan, 1973, also Nepal's first natural World Heritage Site.
